abstract: Whole-genome sequencing identifies focal DNA amplifications with base-pair resolution but cannot determine whether amplified sequences reside on extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA, also known as double minutes) or within chromosomally integrated homogeneously staining regions (HSRs). DNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (DNA-FISH) metaphase spreads remain the gold standard for distinguishing these amplification states at single-cell resolution. Here, we present a detailed protocol for DNA-FISH metaphase spreads using human cancer cell lines, encompassing cell culture, metaphase arrest, hypotonic treatment, fixation, chromosome spreading, fluorescent probe hybridization, and fluorescence imaging. The protocol incorporates intermediate quality-control steps to verify successful chromosome dispersion and optimize metaphase spread quality, making the workflow accessible to laboratories without specialized cytogenetics expertise. Results demonstrate clear visualization of ecDNA and HSR amplification states using locus-specific probes and illustrate common technical artifacts that can affect interpretation. This protocol provides a robust and reproducible approach for studying the structural organization of oncogene amplification in cancer cells.
